content: Helping young people avoid initiating smoking is a critical public health goal, and schools serve as an effective platform to reach nearly all young individuals. School-based smoking prevention programs have been implemented for nearly four decades. This review aimed to evaluate whether such interventions prevent youth from starting smoking and to identify which types of interventions are most effective. Specific factors examined included theoretical approaches, the inclusion of booster sessions, the role of program deliverers, gender-specific effects, and the comparison of multifocal interventions versus those focused solely on smoking prevention. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) where students, classes, schools, or school districts were randomized to intervention or control groups, with a follow-up period of at least six months. Participants were youth aged 5 to 18 years. Interventions consisted of any school-based curricula designed to deter tobacco use, and outcomes measured included rates of never smoking, smoking frequency, number of cigarettes smoked, or smoking indices. A total of 134 studies involving 428,293 participants met the inclusion criteria. These studies were categorized into three groups for analysis: (1) Pure Prevention cohorts, (2) Change in Smoking Behavior over time, and (3) Point Prevalence of Smoking. Pure Prevention Cohorts (Group 1): Forty-nine studies (N = 142,447) were included in this group. At follow-up of one year or less, there was no overall effect of intervention curricula compared to control groups (odds ratio [OR] 0.94, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.85 to 1.05). However, subgroup analysis revealed that combined social competence and social influences curricula significantly reduced the onset of smoking (OR 0.49, 95% CI 0.28 to 0.87). In contrast, interventions focused solely on information (OR 0.12, 95% CI 0.00 to 14.87), social influences (OR 1.00, 95% CI 0.88 to 1.13), or multimodal approaches (OR 0.89, 95% CI 0.73 to 1.08) did not show significant effects. At the longest follow-up, pooled results demonstrated a significant overall effect favoring the intervention (OR 0.88, 95% CI 0.82 to 0.96). Subgroup analyses showed significant effects for social competence curricula (OR 0.52, 95% CI 0.30 to 0.88) and combined social competence and social influences curricula (OR 0.50, 95% CI 0.28 to 0.87). Programs focused solely on information, social influences, or multimodal approaches remained ineffective. Change in Smoking Behavior Over Time (Group 2): Fifteen studies (N = 45,555) were included in this group. At one year or less, there was a small but statistically significant effect favoring the control group (standardized mean difference [SMD] 0.04, 95% CI 0.02 to 0.06). For follow-up periods longer than one year, the effect was statistically nonsignificant (SMD 0.02, 95% CI -0.00 to 0.02). Point Prevalence of Smoking (Group 3): Twenty-five studies reported data on the point prevalence of smoking. However, due to high heterogeneity, data could not be pooled for analysis. Additional Findings: Subgroup analyses for Pure Prevention cohorts showed that at the longest follow-up, interventions delivered by adult presenters had a significant effect (OR 0.88, 95% CI 0.81 to 0.96). There were no significant differences between tobacco-only interventions and multifocal interventions. For curricula with booster sessions, significant effects were observed only for combined social competence and social influences interventions, both at one year or less (OR 0.50, 95% CI 0.26 to 0.96) and at the longest follow-up (OR 0.51, 95% CI 0.27 to 0.96). Limited data on gender differences suggested no overall effect, although one study reported a significant effect of multimodal interventions for male students at one year. Authors' Conclusions: Pure Prevention cohorts demonstrated a significant effect at the longest follow-up, with an average 12% reduction in smoking initiation compared to control groups. However, no overall effect was observed at one year or less. Combined social competence and social influences interventions were effective at both one year and the longest follow-up. Social influences-only programs, multimodal interventions, and information-only approaches were ineffective at all time points. Studies examining Change in Smoking Behavior over time did not show an overall effect, but positive findings were noted for social competence and combined social competence and social influences interventions.
